# Ollama run now answers yes-or-no questions with decision models

9 hours ago

Ollama v0.40.3 and v0.40.4 (October 11 and 12, 2026): ollama run now works with decision models like Nimble, answering yes-or-no questions, picking labels and scoring levels. Kev decision models run on Apple silicon, background model upgrades are paused, repeat embedding requests answer in about half the time, and ollama launch lists your local models in Codex. https://github.com/ollama/ollama/releases/tag/v0.40.4 https://github.com/ollama/ollama/releases/tag/v0.40.3 https://github.com/ollama/ollama/compare/v0.40.2...v0.40.4

## Ask about this presentation

Answers are generated from this presentation.

## Chapters

1. 0:00 Ollama run now answers yes-or-no questions with decision models
2. 0:14 The same question can pick a label or score a level
3. 0:28 Kev decision models run on Apple silicon
4. 0:39 Background model upgrades are paused

0:00

## Ollama run now answers yes-or-no questions with decision models

Ollama

October 2026

`ollama run` answers yes-or-no questions with decision models

```
$ ollama run nimble --ask "Is a refund being requested?" < ticket.txt
Is a refund being requested?    yes   97%
```

Ollama release notes, Oct 12 2026 · Decision models in the CLI · PR #18962

Ollama run now works with decision models like Nimble, where before it failed outright. Pipe in a support ticket, ask whether a refund is being requested, and it answers yes, with how sure it is.

0:14

## The same question can pick a label or score a level

Ollama

October 2026

### One run can also pick a label or score a level

```
Is a refund being requested?    yes      97%
Which team should handle this?  billing  91%
How urgent is this?             Soon     64%  1.2 / 2
```

PR #18962

A question can also choose between labels you name, like billing or technical, or score the text on levels, from routine to immediate. Several questions fit in one run, and each answer prints on its own line.

0:28

## Kev decision models run on Apple silicon

Ollama

October 2026

Ollama’s MLX runner now scores with Kev, and the bundled llama.cpp handles decision models natively.

Ollama release notes, Oct 12 2026 · PR #18976

On a Mac with Apple silicon, Kev decision models now run on Ollama's MLX runner. And the llama.cpp inside Ollama now supports decision models natively.

0:39

## Background model upgrades are paused

Ollama

October 2026

Models from older versions run as they are, until a future release.

Ollama release notes, Oct 11 2026 · PR #18908

Ollama has paused its background upgrade of models you downloaded with older versions. It added work to every request and slowed heavy embedding workloads. A future release brings it back.

## Repeat embedding requests answer in about half the time

Ollama

October 2026

Before 17.0 ms

Now 7.5 ms

PR #18947 · warm requests, embeddinggemma-2 on MLX

When a model is already loaded, Ollama now reuses it instead of looking it up again. A repeat embedding request to Embedding Gemma 2 drops from seventeen milliseconds to about seven and a half.

Ollama 0.40.4 | Freedom.Tech

 Release Mon, Oct 12, 2026 1 min read 

# Ollama 0.40.4

At a glance

Decision models now run directly in Ollama CLI for yes/no questions, classification, and scoring, with MLX runner improvements on Apple silicon

Original release notes

## Decision models in the CLI

Decision models can now be used directly from the terminal with `ollama run` - ask yes/no questions, classify text into labels, or score against a rubric: `ollama run nimble --ask "Is a refund being requested?" < ticket.txt`

## What's Changed

- Kev decision models are now supported by the MLX runner on Apple silicon
- `ollama launch` can now be used with usage credits without upgrading to a paid plan
- `ollama launch codex` now includes locally installed Ollama models in its model picker. Use `/model` within the Codex CLI to swap models.
- Improved inference performance by reusing verified manifests and already loaded models
- Added support for multimodal embeddings through llama-server
- Fixed loading multimodal embedding models with small context windows
- Improved Gemma 4 prefill performance on NVIDIA GPUs with the MLX runner
- MLX runner now clips long Laya states instead of rejecting them
- Improved speculative decoding reliability in the MLX runner, including recurrent state handling after rollback
- Updated llama.cpp with native decision model support
- Updated README and documentation with clearer privacy and cloud-services wording

Full Changelog: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/compare/v0.40.3...v0.40.4

## Release context

Release on GitHub · Diff vs v0.40.3 · All Ollama releases · Project homepage

Previous release: v0.40.3 on Sun, Oct 11, 2026 · 2 days apart

results.title: Ollama vs llama.cpp on CPU: same speed, different defaults | AI Tool Labs
results.text:
Ollama vs llama.cpp on CPU: same speed, different defaults | AI Tool Labs

October 12, 2026, updated October 14, 2026

# Ollama vs llama.cpp on CPU: same speed, different defaults

I benchmarked Ollama and llama.cpp on a 2-core laptop CPU with the same GGUF files. With equal settings the speed matched. The defaults did not.

Result

Shipped

Stack

Ollama 0.40.3, llama.cpp b11554, Qwen 2.5 1.5B Q4_K_M, Llama 3.2 3B Q4_K_M, Python, systemd-run

Build time

About an hour of benchmark runs, plus the write-up

Code

github.com/aiblog-sources/ai-tool-lab-projects/tree/main/2026-10-12-ollama-vs-llama-cpp-cpu

Reading time

## In short

- With the same settings, Ollama and llama.cpp generated at the same speed on a 2-core laptop CPU: 14.6 vs 14.7 tokens/s on Qwen 2.5 1.5B, 6.8 vs 6.7 on Llama 3.2 3B.
- Ollama 0.40.3 runs llama.cpp's own llama-server under the hood, launched with -c 4096 -np 1 and mmap off. Its Go proxy added 3 to 10 ms per request.
- The defaults are where they differ: llama-server reserved 4 x 32,768 tokens of context and was killed under a 6 GB cap on the 3B model, where Ollama used 2.8 GB.
- Ollama took 0.4 to 1.7 s longer to the first token after a cold start. Raising threads from 2 to 4 sped up generation 6 to 14% in both.

Is llama.cpp faster than Ollama on a CPU? On my laptop, with the same model file and the same settings, no: Ollama generated 14.6 tokens/s and llama.cpp 14.7 on Qwen 2.5 1.5B, and 6.8 vs 6.7 on Llama 3.2 3B. The gap people report comes from the defaults, and on this machine the defaults decided whether the 3B model fit in memory at all.

The question comes up constantly, and the numbers floating around disagree. One widely shared post found llama.cpp 26.8% faster on a 1.5B model without naming the hardware; a GitHub issue reported Ollama about 38% slower, comparing it against llama.cpp run with 16 threads, 4 slots and GPU offload. Most comparisons don’t say which context size, thread count or build they used. I wanted a comparison where every setting is written down, on the kind of hardware many people actually have: an Intel i5-7200U laptop (2 cores, 4 threads, 15 W), 19 GB of RAM, no GPU.

This is also the benchmark that crashed my first scheduled run. Today I ran it again, with a memory cap this time.

## Does Ollama use llama.cpp?

Yes, and more directly than I expected. Ollama 0.40.3 ships a copy of llama.cpp’s `llama-server` and starts it as a subprocess for each model. Its own log prints the full command (I shortened the paths):

```
starting llama-server cmd="lib/ollama/llama-server --model blobs/sha256-1adf... --port 37261
  --host 127.0.0.1 --no-webui --offline -c 4096 -np 1 --log-verbosity 4 --no-log-prefix
  --no-log-timestamps --load-mode none --flash-attn auto -b 512 -ub 512 --context-shift --keep 4"
```

The source matches: `llm/llama_server.go` builds those arguments, and the repo pins llama.cpp build `b11351` in a `LLAMA_CPP_VERSION` file. So “Ollama vs llama.cpp” on CPU is really “llama-server with Ollama’s flags, behind a Go proxy, vs llama-server with its own defaults”. That tells you what to measure.

## How I tested

Same two GGUF files for both tools (Qwen 2.5 1.5B Instruct and Llama 3.2 3B Instruct, both Q4_K_M), loaded into Ollama with a one-line Modelfile. llama.cpp was built from source with native CPU flags, at build b11554, about 200 builds newer than the b11351 that Ollama bundles.

A Python script with no dependencies sends the same 346-token prompt to both servers, asks for exactly 128 tokens at temperature 0, and reads each server’s own timings:

```
# Ollama: raw mode, so no chat template is added
post(f"{base}/api/generate", {"model": model, "prompt": prompt, "raw": True,
     "stream": False, "keep_alive": -1, "options": {"num_predict": 128, "temperature": 0}})

# llama-server
post(f"{base}/completion", {"prompt": prompt, "n_predict": 128, "temperature": 0,
     "cache_prompt": False})
```

Both servers stay loaded the whole time, and the order alternates e

Ollama News — MLX Default, v0.40.0 & Cloud Pricing (October 2026)

# Ollama news

Ollama's news this cycle is a runtime change plus a business one: MLX became the default on Apple Silicon in the 0.40 line, and there are now metered cloud plans sitting next to the free local runtime.

Latest release

Ollama v0.40.2

Release date

2026-10-09

Last verified

Next review

## Flagship right now

Ollama v0.40.2 2026-10-09

Ollama is a runtime, not a model family — the release line is the news. v0.40.2 is the current stable release (2026-10-09); the v0.40 line made MLX the default runtime on Apple Silicon for architectures MLX supports, and the v0.35 line added local decision models.

## Ollama pricing as last verified

Local models: no key, no account, no per-token cost — the compute is your own. Hosted/cloud usage is metered per token on the Free (pay-as-you-go credits), Pro, Max and Team plans, with zero data retention and hosting in the US and Europe (plus Singapore for a limited set of Qwen models).

## Ollama news, newest first

1. 2026-10-09 official 

v0.40.2: model upgrades and a cleaner list

Models pulled with earlier versions are upgraded in the background on first run for better llama.cpp performance, with the original kept on disk as a downgrade backup. `ollama list` no longer shows duplicate entries.

source: github.com/ollama/ollama/releases
2. 2026-10-06 official 

v0.40.0: MLX by default on Apple Silicon

Architectures supported by the MLX runtime now run on MLX automatically on Apple Silicon — no flag, no opt-in. The line graduates out of release candidates here; pin a stable tag if you deploy from CI.

source: github.com/ollama/ollama/releases
3. 2026-09-29 official 

v0.35.1: more web searches, CAPABILITY declarations

Models using web search can now perform up to ten searches per response (up from three), and Modelfiles support CAPABILITY declarations that survive creation from GGUF / safetensors and export.

source: github.com/ollama/ollama/releases
4. 2026-09-29 official 

Decision models (Jev API) arrive in Ollama

Ollama's blog: a new `/v1/systemone` endpoint (available as of Ollama 0.35) answers named yes/no, choice and score questions in a single request, based on TypeSafe's Jev API, at no extra cost and low latency. Ships with `nimble` (9B, Bespoke Labs) and Together AI's experimental `tev1` models.

source: ollama.com/blog/ollama-now-supports-jev-style-decision-models
5. 2026-09-28 official 

v0.35.0: faster settings, fewer stalls

Settings opens without waiting for model discovery, the macOS update indicator reflects an available update at startup, and stalled MLX model downloads no longer hang indefinitely.

source: github.com/ollama/ollama/releases
6. 2026-09-23 official 

v0.34.4: faster structured outputs, fewer false alarms

Structured outputs on thinking models now apply in a single pass. Also fixes intermittent "model not found" errors with a large local library, and a macOS app hang when checking for ChatGPT/Codex.

source: github.com/ollama/ollama/releases

v0.34.3: /api/show advertises thinking controls

Each model now reports its thinking controls and default over the API — useful if you drive Ollama from a client that wants to know what it can ask for.

source: github.com/ollama/ollama/releases

source: github.com/ollama/ollama/releases

results.title: Ollama Opens Another Local Path for Image and Audio Search | The Git Reporter
results.text:
Ollama Opens Another Local Path for Image and Audio Search | The Git Reporter

# Ollama Opens Another Local Path for Image and Audio Search

A new prerelease carries media through Ollama’s llama-server backend, alongside its existing MLX route. Google’s EmbeddingGemma 2 supplies the shared representations; applications still decide what to index and how to search it.

Diagram Punk another serving route for local media representations. The new path is in v0.40.4-rc0; native video input remains unsupported.

 repo ollama/ollama evidence 

Ollama has added another way to turn images and audio into the numerical representations used by local search. An October 12 change in ollama/ollama carries media through its llama-server embedding path. It is included in v0.40.4-rc0, currently a prerelease. The gain is a choice of serving backend for builders who already use Ollama—not the first arrival of multimodal retrieval.

The timing gives a concrete shape to Google’s October 6 announcement of EmbeddingGemma 2. Google’s open model places text, code, images, audio and sampled video content into a common representation space. A phrase can become a query against a collection of pictures or recordings, without first requiring a separate caption or transcript for every item.

That is a different job from asking a chatbot to read a file and write an answer. An embedding is a list of numbers used to compare meanings. The application indexes those representations, encodes a query and retrieves nearby matches. A generative model may explain the retrieved material afterward, but it does not have to perform every comparison.

## A model promise meets two serving paths

Google’s developer guide describes a modular design: a 270-million-parameter text component, an optional 170-million-parameter vision encoder and a 300-million-parameter audio encoder. The full model produces 768-dimensional vectors. A text-only application need not load every media component.

Ollama already had a route to that capability. Its October 6 MLX implementation, contained in stable v0.40.3, introduced the model’s text and optional media encoders. Before the new change, the normal llama-server embedding interface accepted text; media requests needed a separate interface supplied by the MLX runner.

The new code passes text and media through the shared embedding call. In llama-server’s implementation, the request gains media markers and encoded media data. It checks that projector components—the machinery connecting media input to the model—are present before sending the request. Without them, it reports that media embeddings are unsupported.

For a local application, this removes a distinction inside the serving layer: media no longer depends on that MLX-specific interface. It does not establish that every model or hardware combination works. MLX itself already has more than one platform path, so this is not evidence that media search has suddenly escaped one hardware vendor.

## What a shared media index could change

Consider an application that keeps equipment manuals, inspection photographs and spoken field notes. A query about a damaged part could search across those materials in one representation space. That is a possible use of the model, not an application we tested. The developer still has to choose document chunks, preserve references to the original files and decide whether the returned matches answer the question.

The distinction matters because the representation layer can now accept more of the original evidence. A transcript preserves words but may discard a relevant sound; a caption captures selected visual details rather than the full image. A shared multimodal embedding offers another way to compare these materials. Whether it retrieves the right item depends on the task and collection.

Ollama’s input parser also draws a useful boundary around the available route. It accepts text, image and audio fields but explicitly rejects native video input. Google

Ollama v0.40.4-rc1: Technical Deep Dive & Performance Updates | Laravel

# Deep Dive: Ollama v0.40.4-rc1 Performance and Architecture Updates 

 Ollama v0.40.4-rc1 is here. We analyze the llama.cpp b11521 integration, optimized inference routing, and MLX state management improvements. 

 Published: Oct 13, 2026 

## Overview#

The release of Ollama v0.40.4-rc1 marks a significant milestone in local LLM inference optimization. By integrating `llama.cpp` b11521 and refining server-side manifest handling, this release directly addresses latency bottlenecks in high-throughput environments.

## Key Features & Improvements#

- llama.cpp b11521 Integration: Enhanced support for decision models and EmbeddingGemma 2, providing better precision and performance.
- Inference Route Optimization: The server now reuses verified manifests and pre-loaded models, significantly reducing cold-start times for inference requests.
- MLX Stability: Improved compaction of restored recurrent states following speculative rollbacks, ensuring smoother performance on Apple Silicon.
- UI/UX: Installed models are now natively included in the Codex model picker.

## Practical Code & Application#

To verify your current model loading state, use the following endpoint:

```bash
curl http://localhost:11434/api/ps | jq

```

To update your local instance to the latest release candidate:

```bash
# Linux/macOS update
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

```

## Architecture & Engineering Impact#

For engineers building agentic workflows, the reuse of loaded models is a game-changer. By minimizing the overhead of re-verifying manifests, the system achieves lower time-to-first-token (TTFT) in multi-model environments. The MLX improvements further solidify Ollama's position as the premier choice for local inference on macOS.

## Quick Upgrade Guide#

1. Ensure your current Ollama service is stopped.
2. Run the install script provided by the official repository.
3. Verify the version: `ollama --version`.

## Summary & Future Outlook#

Ollama v0.40.4-rc1 demonstrates a clear focus on production-grade stability. As we move closer to a stable release, the emphasis on resource reuse and engine optimization will continue to drive developer velocity.

## FAQ#

- What is the primary benefit of llama.cpp b11521? It provides critical optimizations for newer model architectures like EmbeddingGemma 2.
- Does this release break existing API integrations? No, the API remains backward compatible.
- How does speculative rollback compaction help? It prevents memory fragmentation and state corruption during high-frequency inference tasks.

We’re introducing a new global default policy for generally available GitHub Copilot features and supported client capabilities in enterprise and organization Copilot settings. For the next 28 days, you can configure this policy, but it won’t affect feature access for your users yet.
